extracted.intended_audience: general readers and practitioners seeking an introduction to and practical guidance for Stoic philosophy (including those who want to write a personal Stoic handbook)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for understanding Stoicism as a philosophical worldview and for practicing it in daily life, including steps for composing a personal handbook of Stoic exercises and reminders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoicism as a philosophy (discipline of love for wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism is a philosophy: a discipline of love (philos) for wisdom (sophia), primarily a contemplative (theoretical) knowledge of nature and humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize philosophical reflection, not just techniques. The ancient Stoics sought knowledge of the Cosmos and human nature; practice must be rooted in understanding, not mere rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic worldview: Nature is rational and good (logos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoics perceive the world as essentially harmonic, governed by a rational principle (logos); the cosmic order is essentially good and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a cosmovision that sees natural laws and order; this underpins Stoic spirituality and justifies ethical aims. Avoid interpretations that discard the Stoic conception of nature and the divine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between speech and action (integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoics pursue harmony between speech and action and maintain high moral standards of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate integrity: ensure your behavior matches your professed principles. The book stresses being a moral example through coherence of word and deed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratic self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous self-examination of beliefs to discard false beliefs, purify the soul, and achieve eudaimonia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly scrutinize opinions and moral commitments (in the Socratic manner). This is foundational: examine what you take as true and correct errors to progress morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of theory and practice (Cynic influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism emphasizes the connection between philosophical theory and lived practice: philosophy as a way of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to be a 'living embodiment' of Stoic principles. The text repeatedly urges harmonization of theoretical insight with concrete moral behavior (praxis), influenced by Cynic models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Epictetus's three topics (desire, action, assent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize Stoic practice around Epictetus’s three topics: the topic of desire, the topic of action, and the topic of assent (judgement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame exercises and reflections using these three domains—manage desires, perform correct actions, and govern assent/judgement—this structure is central to the book's practical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing Stoicism to performance/resilience (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce Stoicism to mere efficiency, resilience training, or a Silicon Valley-style self-help toolkit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book warns against modern movements that treat Stoicism as productivity/resilience hacks. Preserve its philosophical depth and communal/social aims rather than turning it into anti-intellectual prescriptive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Stoic spirituality and worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the Stoic 'vision of wholeness'—a spirituality that sees the self as reflecting the divine order—rather than stripping Stoicism of its worldview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice includes cultivating a sense that the soul reflects cosmic order; this spiritual/cosmic dimension differentiates traditional Stoicism from purely instrumental adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the tenets at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Having the Tenets at Hand (keep Stoic principles accessible for regular consultation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make core Stoic principles immediately available (notes, reminders, short manual) to support frequent recollection and application throughout daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular examination of conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination of Conscience: perform routine self-review of actions, judgments, and moral progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured reflection (daily or periodic) to review choices and align future behavior with Stoic ideals; this is a central recommended practice in composing a personal handbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility: don't show off or consider yourself too wise
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t show off or consider yourself too wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pride and the pretense of wisdom. The book highlights humility as essential: the Stoic must not only speak virtue but live it without seeking ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-communion and self-forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in honest internal dialogue and practice forgiving oneself for moral lapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance rigorous self-examination with self-compassion; handle failures as occasions for correction rather than self-condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly practice gratitude as part of Stoic training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate appreciation for what you have and what nature provides; gratitude supports resilience and right judgment about value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish vices, virtues, and passions; manage passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and classify vices, virtues, and passions in Stoic terms and use that taxonomy to manage emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn Stoic categories (what is good, bad, indifferent) and identify which passions are to be moderated or transformed; the book includes chapters and examples on specific passions (e.g., wrath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and cultivate 'good passions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize emotions that can be rightly ordered ('good passions') and cultivate them appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism does not demand eradication of all feeling—some properly informed emotions aligned with virtue are endorsed. The manual distinguishes these from irrational passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific management of anger (wrath)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address wrath explicitly: understand its nature and apply Stoic strategies to control it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection, judgment correction, and role-expectation techniques to defuse anger; the text treats wrath as a paradigmatic passion to be managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume social roles responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Take up and fulfill the social roles you must assume (family, civic, professional) in accordance with Stoic duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism prescribes acting well within the roles life assigns; ethics is social and political, not merely individualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time wisely (value of life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use wisely the time you are given—time is precious and must be well invested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent injunctions (from Seneca quoted in the book): plan days as if they might be your last, avoid wasting time, and reserve time for philosophy and self-care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the awareness of impermanence (everything will pass)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the perspective that all things pass—use transience both to free yourself from attachments and to celebrate moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice premeditation of losses (premeditatio malorum) and gratitude for present goods; this tempering of attachment helps right-valued responses to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and value friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is a Stoic good; cultivate supportive, virtuous relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop bonds that encourage moral progress; the Stoics valued social ties as part of living in accordance with nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice what you preach (avoid hypocrisy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prescribe appropriate actions to others if you yourself practice inappropriate actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musonius Rufus’s warning: moral authority requires personal exemplarity; avoid being an instructor who fails to live according to the counsel offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for a noble death
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to accept and, if necessary, pursue a noble death—cultivate readiness and dignity in the face of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seneca and other Stoics recommend reflecting on mortality to orient action and value; 'grasp a noble death while it is possible' underlines active preparation rather than morbid fixation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy is dialogical: develop through dialogue and debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical exercise is dialogical: philosophy develops through conversation, critique, and debate with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with communities, read widely, and dialog with peers to refine understanding; the text recounts the historical role of schools and debates in shaping Stoic doctrine.
